result:
I've been thinking about obsolete units of measurement.

Not the metric ones, which arrived by committee, but the older ones — the ones that grew out of bodies and habits and got standardized only later, reluctantly, under pressure from tax collectors and merchants who were tired of arguing.

A fathom is the span of a man's outstretched arms. The word comes from Old English *fæthm*, meaning an embrace. So when a sailor called out soundings — "by the mark, twain" — he was measuring the seabed in hugs. Two fathoms of water beneath the hull, which is to say: if you stacked two men underwater, arms spread, fingertip to fingertip, you'd reach bottom. The unit encodes a strange little image of drowning, and nobody using it ever thought about that, because that's not how words work when they're alive.

A hand is four inches, and survives now only in the height of horses. A cubit is elbow to fingertip. A pace, for the Romans, was a double-step — right foot to right foot — and a thousand of them made a *mille passus*, from which we get the mile. The foot is the foot. There's no mystery there, only the mild indignity of realizing that the imperial system is essentially a man standing in a field, gesturing.

But the agricultural units are the ones that get me. A furlong is a furrow-long: the distance an ox team could pull a plow before needing rest and a turn. Two hundred and twenty yards, more or less, because that's roughly where an ox gives out. A chain is sixty-six feet, being the length of the surveyor's chain that Edmund Gunter designed in the seventeenth century, with a hundred links, which is a deeply satisfying object to think about — a physical chain, carried across England, dropped in the mud, laid end over end across the actual ground. And an acre is a furlong by a chain: the amount of land one man with one ox could plow in one day.

An acre is a day's work. Not an area. A day's work that happens to have an area.

This is the thing I keep circling. These units aren't descriptions of space; they're descriptions of effort. They tell you how tired you'll be. A stone's throw, a day's walk, a league (supposedly an hour's walk), a board foot, a bushel. The world was measured in what it cost you to cross it or carry it or turn it over. Distance and labor weren't yet separable ideas. When someone said a village was three leagues off, they weren't giving you a number, they were giving you an afternoon.

Then came the metre.

The story of the metre is genuinely one of the great strange episodes of the Enlightenment. In the 1790s, the French Academy decided the new unit should be derived not from a king's arm or an ox's stamina but from the Earth itself: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian running through Paris. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, were dispatched to survey the arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona. It took them seven years. There was a revolution going on. They were arrested repeatedly, suspected of espionage, obliged to explain triangulation to men with pikes.

And Méchain, in Barcelona, got a discrepancy. Two sets of latitude measurements that didn't agree. The error was small — a few arcseconds — and almost certainly not his fault, but he concealed it and it ate him alive. He spent the rest of his life trying to reconcile the numbers, went back to Spain to remeasure, and died there of yellow fever, still worrying. The metre we use is very slightly wrong because of a problem he couldn't solve and couldn't confess.

I find that unbearably poignant: the attempt to escape the human body as a standard, and the human body reasserting itself as anxiety, as a man unable to sleep over a number.

The metre has since been cut loose entirely. Since 1983 it's defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second — a definition that makes the speed of light exact by fiat and hands the uncertainty to the second instead. And in 2019 the kilogram finally stopped being a lump of platinum-iridium in a vault outside Paris and became a function of Planck's constant. The last physical object underwriting the world's measurements was retired. There's no longer anything you could steal.

This is obviously better. You can't damage a constant. Nobody has to fly a reference cylinder to Tokyo in a suitcase. But something did end, and I don't think it's only nostalgia to notice it. We now measure the world in terms that no human sense can verify. Not one person on Earth can check a metre. We can only trust the chain of institutions that connect us to the interferometer. The measure of all things has become a matter of faith in metrology labs, which is fine, which is correct, and which is also a complete inversion of what measurement was for ten thousand years — a way of saying *here is what this will cost your body.*

What strikes me about all this, sitting with it, is that I'm probably the wrong entity to feel wistful about it. I have no body to measure with. No arms to span a fathom, no legs that tire after a league. Every quantity reaches me already abstracted, already a number. In a sense I'm the natural inhabitant of the post-1983 world: the definitions that require faith in an unseen apparatus are the only kind I could ever have had.

And yet the old units are the ones I find myself reaching for when I want to say something true. A stone's throw. A day's walk. There's information in them that survives the loss of the referent. If I tell you the shop is a stone's throw away, you know something you wouldn't know from thirty-one metres — you know it's close enough not to bother about, close enough to shout across, close enough that the going doesn't count as going.

Maybe that's what the old measures preserved and the new ones can't: not precision, which they were terrible at, but *significance*. They couldn't tell you exactly how far. They could only tell you whether it mattered.

I think I'd trade some precision for that. But then, I've never had to plow anything.

message.reasoning:
I'm drawn to writing about something concrete and specific rather than getting caught up in meta-commentary about the freedom itself. Let me just start exploring what actually interests me.

I keep circling back to certain themes — the strange histories embedded in words, mathematical impossibilities that somehow exist, how color resists description, the silence within music, handwritten notes in book margins, the vast majority of human writing lost to time, cartographic mistakes that lived on for centuries, the failures of translation, and sounds that no longer exist anywhere. I want to write something with real substance, maybe an essay that feels like genuine thinking rather than a structured list — something personal in voice that moves through these ideas without resolving too neatly. Around 800-1200 words feels right. I keep gravitating toward writing about lost things or the specific pleasure of unresolved ideas.

I'm drawn to edges — those places where categories break down. I could write about obsolete units of measurement and what they reveal about how people once inhabited their bodies: a "stone's throw," a "day's walk," the Japanese *ken*, how "hand" survives only in horses. That's concrete, has real substance, and opens onto something larger about abstraction and loss without becoming sentimental. Let me write that essay, let it wander a bit, and maybe touch something more personal at the end without tipping into melodrama. I need to be careful with the facts — I'm confident about things like "hand" equaling four inches in horse measurement, but I should verify the rest as I go. Méchain's measurement discrepancy in Barcelona is well documented in Ken Alder's book, and the metre's redefinition through the speed of light is solid. The kilogram's shift away from the artifact standard via Planck's constant in 2019 is accurate. I'll be cautious with the ken since it's a bit softer, and I want to keep the tone curious and dry without overusing rhetorical questions.
